items.rule: A perfect square is an integer that can be written as the square of another integer.
In prime factorisation, pair identical prime factors and take one factor from every pair outside the square root.
A perfect cube has every prime exponent divisible by 3.
Extract the largest perfect-square factor from inside a square root.
Only like surds can be directly added or subtracted.
Multiply the coefficients and multiply the radicands, then simplify.
For positive radicands, divide inside one root or rationalise if a surd remains in the denominator.
Multiply numerator and denominator by the same surd to remove a square-root denominator.
The conjugates of a+√b and a−√b multiply to a rational expression.
An irrational number cannot be written as a ratio of two integers in lowest terms.

concepts.title: 1. Perfect Squares & Square Roots
concepts.subtitle: Recognising and Computing Exact Roots
concepts.summary: Perfect squares arise by squaring integers. Square roots can be found by recognising known squares or by prime factorisation, while non-perfect squares can be approximated or found using the long-division method.

points.text: Perfect Square: A number such as 1, 4, 9, 16, ..., 225 that equals an integer squared.
Prime Factorisation: Pair identical prime factors and take one member of every pair outside the square root.
Non-perfect Squares: Their square roots are irrational and can be approximated using long division or numerical estimation.
Range Check: To estimate √n, locate consecutive perfect squares around n.

concepts.trap: Remember that √a denotes the principal non-negative square root. For example, √49=7, although both 7² and (−7)² equal 49.

concepts.title: 2. Cubes & Cube Roots
concepts.subtitle: Recognising Perfect Cubes
concepts.summary: A perfect cube is the cube of an integer. Cube roots can be found by recognising familiar cubes or by prime factorisation, grouping identical prime factors in threes.

points.text: Prime Factors: Group identical prime factors in triples when finding a cube root.
Cube Root: The notation $\sqrt[3]{n}$ represents the real number whose cube is n.
Sign Rule: Cube roots preserve sign, so $\sqrt[3]{-a}=-\sqrt[3]{a}$.

concepts.trap: Do not confuse cube-root grouping with square-root grouping. Cube factors must be grouped in threes, not pairs.

concepts.title: 3. Surds & Irrational Numbers
concepts.subtitle: Simplifying Exact Radical Expressions
concepts.summary: A surd is an irrational root expression in exact radical form. Simplify it by extracting perfect-square factors, then combine only like surds.

points.text: Surd: A radical expression that represents an irrational number, such as $\sqrt{2}$ or $3\sqrt{5}$.
Extract Squares: Rewrite the radicand as a product containing the largest possible perfect square.
Like Surds: Terms such as $3\sqrt{7}$ and $5\sqrt{7}$ can be combined because their radical parts match.
Unlike Surds: $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}$ cannot be added into a single simpler surd.
Exact Form: A surd keeps an exact irrational value instead of replacing it with a rounded decimal.

concepts.trap: Do not combine unlike surds. For example, √2+√3 is already simplified; it is not √5.

concepts.title: 4. Rationalising the Denominator
concepts.subtitle: Removing Surds from the Denominator
concepts.summary: A rational denominator contains no irrational radical. Multiply by a suitable expression equal to 1: the same surd for a single radical denominator, or the conjugate for a binomial denominator.

points.text: Single Surd: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same surd.
Binomial Surd: Multiply by the conjugate, changing the sign between the two terms.
Difference of Squares: $(a+\sqrt{b})(a-\sqrt{b})=a^2-b$ gives a rational denominator.
Final Form: After rationalising, simplify the numerator and denominator completely.

concepts.trap: Do not rationalise by changing only the sign in the original denominator. The conjugate must multiply both numerator and denominator.
